The incubation period of the Chinese pond heron (Ardeola bacchus) lasts approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 38 °C [T = 38 °C], a value consistent with the developmental rates of other ardeid species of similar egg size. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge at a remarkably low initial wet weight of only 17 grams [Ww0 = 17 grams], a mass that underscores the substantial investment in post-hatching parental care required to bridge the gap to independence. This modest neonatal mass is typical for herons, which produce highly dependent chicks that rely entirely on regurgitated food from both parents during the first weeks of life. The rapid growth trajectory that follows is fueled by intensive provisioning, and the brood is usually complete within a few days of the first hatch, ensuring synchronous development among siblings. Field observations consistently report that the timing of hatching is closely tied to local prey abundance, with peak emergence coinciding with the seasonal availability of small fish and amphibians.

Juvenile birds undergo a critical developmental milestone when they achieve their first sustained flight. This fledging event typically occurs approximately 30 days after hatching [tx = approximately 30 days after hatching] under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species (40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]), a duration that aligns with the post-natal development rates observed in related bitterns and egrets. During this period, the pin-feathered chick transforms into a fully feathered fledgling capable of short foraging flights, though it remains dependent on parental food deliveries for several additional weeks. The substantial mass gain from the 17 gram [Ww0 = 17 gram] hatchling to the fledging stage is a testimony to the efficient conversion of prey biomass into somatic tissue. This growth phase is energetically demanding, and the parents must increase their foraging effort markedly to meet the chicks' daily caloric requirements. The achievement of flight marks the beginning of the transition from a stationary nestling to a more mobile juvenile, exploring the surrounding wetland habitat.

Onset of sexual maturity in the Chinese pond heron is a gradual process that culminates in the ability to breed. Available data indicate that puberty, defined by the initiation of gonadal development and complete feather maturation, is reached at 90 days after hatching [tp = 90 days after hatching] when maintained at the elevated body temperature characteristic of active physiology (40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]). This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive competence is adaptive for a migratory species that must breed within a compressed seasonal window. Young birds typically disperse from their natal colonies before reaching this age, and the subsequent weeks involve extensive exploration of potential breeding territories. The maturation of the gonads is accompanied by the development of the distinctive white breeding plumage and the strengthening of the facial wattles, signals used in mate attraction and territorial defense. Despite reaching puberty, most individuals defer their first nesting attempt until they have established a secure feeding territory.

The age at first successful reproduction represents a distinct life-history milestone following puberty. Field records from monitored breeding colonies show that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 1.5 years [tR = approximately 1.5 years] under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods (40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]). This one-and-a-half-year delay between reaching sexual maturity and initiating a first clutch is ecologically significant, as it allows young adults to accumulate body reserves and gain experience in locating productive foraging sites. First-time breeders often produce smaller clutches and experience lower fledging success compared to older, more experienced pairs. The breeding season is timed to coincide with the monsoon rains that flood shallow wetlands, creating abundant feeding opportunities for chicks. Most individuals that survive to this age will pair monogamously for the duration of the breeding season.

Regarding reproductive output, females typically lay 4 to 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 6 eggs per clutch], and they can produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year] under favorable environmental conditions. This reproductive strategy is typical of medium-sized herons, enabling them to capitalize on extended periods of high prey availability. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 10.1 years [am = approximately 10.1 years], again under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods (40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]), a relatively modest longevity compared to larger, more slowly reproducing herons. The basal metabolic rate sustaining these life-history processes has been measured at 176.63 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 176.63 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at an ambient temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], reflecting the high energetic cost of maintaining active thermoregulation in a warm climate. The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult females is 280 grams [Wwi = 280 grams], whereas adult males reach a larger ultimate wet weight of 332 grams [Wwi = 332 grams], a sexual size dimorphism that is common among ardeids.
